slides.text: In 1970, a robot in Eindhoven leaned toward quiet voices and drew back from shouting.
The sculptor Edward Ihnatowicz built it for Philips’ exhibition hall: a steel skeleton on hydraulics, taller than anyone who came to see it.
Four microphones and two radar units in its head picked up sound and movement in the room.
Gentle sounds drew its head toward a visitor. Loud ones made it pull back.
In 1974 it was taken down, and for years people in Eindhoven believed it had been destroyed.
In fact, its steel skeleton spent more than forty years standing outdoors in Zeeland, in the Netherlands.
In 2017, a university in Kraków bought it and restored it to working order.
